articles.title: I Built a Transaction Guard That Has to Prove Its Own Decisions
articles.excerpt: Written for the zkVerify Agent Games Season 01 Creator Track. #AgentGames On BNB Chain, new tokens and free mints show up every day. Every one of them asks you to sign something. Your wallet shows you…
articles.body: Written for the zkVerify Agent Games Season 01 Creator Track. #AgentGames The signature is the attack surface On BNB Chain, new tokens and free mints show up every day. Every one of them asks you to sign something. Your wallet shows you a hex string and a button. You are supposed to decide, from that hex, whether the transaction is safe. Most people cannot. The failure modes are not exotic. They are the same three patterns, over and over: An approve() call with the amount set to uint256 max. You meant to approve 100 tokens. You approved all of them, forever. A setApprovalForAll(true) hidden inside a mint flow. One click and every NFT in the wallet can move.
articles.author: GreyArch

articles.title: LogTreeDB: Building a Crash-Safe, Zero-Dependency Document Database from Scratch in C++17
articles.excerpt: Author: Praveen Kumar Executive Summary & The Core Question Databases are often treated as black boxes. When application developers need a document store, they default to MongoDB; when they need an em…
articles.body: Author: Praveen Kumar Date: November 2026 Executive Summary & The Core Question Databases are often treated as black boxes. When application developers need a document store, they default to MongoDB; when they need an embedded engine, they grab SQLite or RocksDB. But under high-concurrency write workloads requiring strict physical durability (fsync on every acknowledged write), traditional database designs encounter severe architectural bottlenecks—most notably Write Amplification (WAF) and Random I/O Thrashing. LogTreeDB is a crash-safe, multi-threaded document database written from absolute scratch in modern C++17 without a single third-party dependency.
articles.author: PRAVEEN KUMAR

articles.body: You work out the structure of next week's presentation with one AI. The next day you ask a different AI to build the slides, and it has no idea what structure you decided on. Pasting the conversation in works. But you can only paste what you remember at that moment, and the decision stays split across each AI's chat history. I wanted what you decide to stay in a note on your side. Graphium notes live in your own folder, so I made the outside AI come to those notes. The connection uses MCP, a common standard for connecting AI apps to outside tools. In the desktop app, open Settings → AI → Use your notes from other AI assistants and press Register on the row for the AI you use. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex and the ChatGPT desktop app can all be registered from this screen.

Most "block AI bots" advice lumps them together, which can quietly remove you from AI answers you'd want to be in. Three kinds of AI bots Training crawlers collect pages to train models: GPTBot (OpenAI), ClaudeBot (Anthropic), Google-Extended (Gemini), Applebot-Extended , meta-externalagent , Amazonbot , CCBot (Common Crawl) and Bytespider (ByteDance). AI search crawlers index pages so assistants can cite you: OAI-SearchBot , Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot . User-triggered fetchers open one page because someone asked about it: ChatGPT-User , Claude-User and Perplexity-User . Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended aren't crawlers at all.

articles.title: PostgreSQL Fix Requires Server Updates and Rebuilding C Extensions
articles.excerpt: Updating PostgreSQL alone is insufficient to fully address a type confusion vulnerability that allows database users with object creation privileges to execute code on the server. According to The Hac…
articles.body: Updating PostgreSQL alone is insufficient to fully address a type confusion vulnerability that allows database users with object creation privileges to execute code on the server. According to The Hacker News, administrators must also rebuild every installed extension written in C to obtain full protection. Scope and exploitation status The executed code runs with the privileges of the operating system account running PostgreSQL. This establishes the impact described in the article; it does not establish execution with the operating system’s highest administrative privileges. Researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit and demonstrated it on PostgreSQL 18.6. However, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group has not reported any attacks using the vulnerability.

articles.title: How to Fuzzy Match in Google Sheets (3 Ways)
articles.excerpt: Google Sheets has no built-in fuzzy match. VLOOKUP, MATCH and XLOOKUP only find text that is identical, so "Inytech" will never find "Initech", and "ACME Pty. Ltd" will never find "Acme Pty Ltd". This…
articles.body: Google Sheets has no built-in fuzzy match. VLOOKUP, MATCH and XLOOKUP only find text that is identical, so "Inytech" will never find "Initech", and "ACME Pty. Ltd" will never find "Acme Pty Ltd". This page shows three ways to fix that, starting with the ones that need no add-on. The problem in one example You have a clean master list of customers with IDs, and a messy list from another system. You want the ID next to every messy name. Master list (columns D and E): Initech, 101 Umbrella Corp, 102 Acme Pty Ltd, 103 Globex Corporation, 104 Messy names (column A, starting at A2): ACME Pty. Ltd Inytech Corp Umbrella Globex A normal VLOOKUP returns #N/A for all four. Each one fails for a different reason: punctuation, a typo, word order and a shortened name.

articles.body: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean.
